name: Jonathan Edwards
life_summary: Jonathan Edwards was born on 5 October 1703 at East Windsor, Connecticut, the only son among the eleven children of the Rev. Timothy Edwards and Esther Stoddard Edwards. He entered the Connecticut Collegiate School (Yale) in 1716, took his B.A. in 1720 and stayed on for graduate study until 1722. Between 1722 and 1726 he preached for about eight months to an English Presbyterian congregation in New York City, briefly settled at Bolton, Connecticut, and then served as a tutor at Yale. In 1726 he went to Northampton, Massachusetts, to assist his grandfather Solomon Stoddard, was ordained there in February 1727, married Sarah Pierpont that July, and became senior pastor when Stoddard died in February 1729. His Northampton ministry included a local revival that began in December 1734 and the wider awakening of 1740–42, during which he preached "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" at Enfield on 8 July 1741. After he pressed for stricter qualifications for communion, the Northampton church dismissed him on 22 June 1750, and from 1751 he served as pastor and missionary at Stockbridge, where he wrote Freedom of the Will (published 1754). He took office as president of the College of New Jersey at Princeton on 16 February 1758 and died there on 22 March 1758 of complications from a smallpox inoculation.

phases.label: East Windsor childhood
phases.summary: Grew up in the East Windsor parsonage of his father, the Rev. Timothy Edwards, the only son among eleven children, and was educated at home in the Bible, theology, classics and ancient languages. The Yale chronology records an awakening at East Windsor in March–May 1712.

phases.label: Yale student years
phases.summary: Student at the Connecticut Collegiate School (Yale) at Wethersfield and New Haven, taking his B.A. in May 1720 and continuing graduate study at New Haven until May 1722. He had pleurisy in his last undergraduate year and, by the Yale chronology's dating, a conversion experience at East Windsor in summer 1721.

phases.label: Early pulpits and tutorship
phases.summary: Preached to an English Presbyterian congregation in New York City (August 1722–April 1723), received his M.A. in September 1723, and agreed to settle as pastor at Bolton, Connecticut (November 1723), leaving in May 1724. He then served as a tutor at Yale from June 1724 until September 1726, with an illness in September–December 1725.
phases.place: New York City; Bolton and New Haven, Connecticut

phases.label: Early Northampton pastorate
phases.summary: Began preaching at Northampton, Massachusetts, in October 1726, was ordained assistant to his grandfather Solomon Stoddard in February 1727, married Sarah Pierpont in July 1727, and became senior pastor when Stoddard died in February 1729. He was ill in spring 1729 and suffered a physical collapse that June; his first four children were born between 1728 and 1734.

phases.label: Northampton revival years
phases.summary: As pastor at Northampton he saw the Connecticut Valley revivals begin in December 1734, published A Faithful Narrative (London 1737; corrected Boston edition 1738), and hosted George Whitefield in October 1740. During the awakening of 1740–42 he preached widely, including at Enfield in July 1741, and defended the revivals in print.
phases.place: Northampton, Massachusetts (with preaching journeys in New England)

sources.label: Jonathan Edwards Center at Yale – Chronology of Edwards' Life and Writings (K. Minkema)
Jonathan Edwards Center at Yale – Biography

phases.label: Late Northampton and dismissal
phases.summary: Still pastor at Northampton, he preached (1742–43) the sermon series later published as Religious Affections (1746), cared for David Brainerd until his death in 1747, and lost his daughter Jerusha in 1748. From 1749 he was in conflict with his church over qualifications for communion, which ended in his dismissal on 22 June 1750.

sources.label: Jonathan Edwards Center at Yale – Chronology of Edwards' Life and Writings (K. Minkema)
Jonathan Edwards Center at Yale – Biography

phases.label: Stockbridge mission years
phases.summary: After supply preaching at Northampton and elsewhere, he was called to Stockbridge in February 1751 and installed in August 1751 as pastor to its English and Indian congregations, serving about 150 Mahican and Mohawk families. There he wrote Freedom of the Will (published 1754) and Original Sin (completed May 1757), amid frontier war and a long illness from July 1754.

sources.label: Jonathan Edwards Center at Yale – Chronology of Edwards' Life and Writings (K. Minkema)
Jonathan Edwards Center at Yale – Biography

phases.label: Princeton presidency
phases.summary: After his son-in-law Aaron Burr died in September 1757, the College of New Jersey offered him its presidency. Released from Stockbridge on 4 January 1758, he took office at Princeton on 16 February and died there on 22 March 1758.

corrections: Checked every date against the Minkema chronology PDF, the Yale biography and family pages, ConnecticutHistory.org, the Princeton & Slavery page and the Nassau Church Princeton Cemetery biography. All the biographer's main dates held up. Note: the Yale edwards.yale.edu pages have an expired HTTPS certificate but load over plain http, so the URLs are kept.

Princeton phase: replaced the Princeton & Slavery source with the Nassau Church Princeton Cemetery bio, because Princeton & Slavery gives Edwards's death as 23 March 1758, which conflicts with the other sources (22 March).
Presidency-offer event (29 Sept 1757): now credited to the Yale chronology, because Princeton & Slavery dates the trustees' letter 19 October 1757.

Enfield sermon event: replaced the general ConnecticutHistory.org article with its 'Today in History: July 8' page, which states the 8 July 1741 date directly. Changed 'published in Boston later that year' to 'shortly afterwards', following the chronology.
Death event: added the Nassau Church Princeton Cemetery bio as an independent source for 22 March 1758 at Princeton, and added his burial in Princeton Cemetery.
Top-level sources: replaced Princeton & Slavery (conflicting death date) with the Nassau Church Princeton Cemetery bio.
Birth event: swapped the Yale Biography source for Yale Family Life. The Biography page only says 'fifth of eleven children'; Family Life states he was the only son (ten daughters and one son).
Marriage event: removed 'daughter of the late Rev. James Pierpont' because the cited pages do not say it in the marriage context. Kept 'eleven children, three sons and eight daughters' (Family Life).
1720 event: made the start of graduate studies exact (3 October 1720, per the chronology).
1729 event and phase: made the timing of the illness exact (April–May 1729 illness, June collapse) instead of 'later that year'.
1734 event: made the timing of A Divine and Supernatural Light exact (August 1734).

Phase 'Early pulpits and tutorship': the Bolton entry now says he agreed to settle in November 1723 and left in May 1724. The late-1725 illness is now dated September–December 1725, per the chronology.
Phase 'Northampton revival years': added that a corrected Boston edition of the Faithful Narrative came out in 1738.
Phase 'Late Northampton and dismissal': dated the Religious Affections sermon series to 1742–43, per the chronology.
Phase 'Stockbridge mission years': Original Sin completion made exact (May 1757); illness start given as July 1754.
Phase 'Princeton presidency': place changed to 'Stockbridge, Massachusetts; Princeton, New Jersey', because he stayed at Stockbridge until January 1758.

Life summary: added the eight-month length of the New York stint, the 1722 end of graduate study, the exact revival start (December 1734), the exact Enfield date, and the exact date he took office at Princeton; wording kept factual.
Checked and not used: Wikipedia puts his dismissal from Northampton in October 1751, which conflicts with the primary chronology (22 June 1750), so it was not adopted or cited.
